powers.title: Declare war
powers.prompt: Who has the power to declare war?
powers.body: Only Congress can declare war — Article I, Section 8.

powers.title: Print money
powers.prompt: Who has the power to print and coin money?
powers.body: The Constitution gives Congress the power to coin money; states are forbidden to.

powers.title: Make treaties
powers.prompt: Who has the power to make treaties with other countries?
powers.body: The President makes treaties with Senate approval — states may not.

powers.title: Create an army
powers.prompt: Who has the power to create and maintain an army and navy?
powers.body: Raising and supporting armies is a federal power of Congress.

powers.title: Regulate interstate commerce
powers.prompt: Who regulates trade between the states?
powers.body: The Commerce Clause puts trade between states under federal control.

powers.title: Driver's licenses
powers.body: Licensing drivers is a classic reserved power of the states.

powers.title: Public schools
powers.body: Education is run by states and their local districts.

powers.title: Run elections
powers.prompt: Who administers elections — even federal ones?
powers.body: States run the polls, count the votes, and certify results.

powers.title: Zoning and land use
powers.prompt: Who approves zoning and land use?
powers.body: Zoning is state and local business — the fair itself needed a permit.

powers.title: Police and fire protection
powers.prompt: Who provides police and fire departments?
powers.body: Public safety is a reserved power exercised by states and localities.

powers.title: Collect taxes
powers.prompt: Who has the power to collect taxes?
powers.body: Both. April 15 exists at every level of government.

powers.title: Establish courts
powers.prompt: Who has the power to establish courts?
powers.body: There are federal courts and state courts — two full ladders of justice.

powers.title: Build roads
powers.prompt: Who has the power to build roads?
powers.body: Interstates are federal-aided, state-built; your street is local. Everyone paves.

powers.title: Make and enforce laws
powers.prompt: Who has the power to make and enforce laws?
powers.body: Congress legislates for the nation; every state legislature does the same at home.

duties.prompt: Name one responsibility that is only for United States citizens.
duties.body: Jury duty and the federal ballot belong to citizens alone.

duties.prompt: Name one right that is only for United States citizens.
duties.body: Citizens alone may vote in federal elections and run for federal office.

duties.prompt: How old do citizens have to be to vote for President?
duties.body: The 26th Amendment set the voting age at 18.

duties.prompt: When must all men register for the Selective Service?
duties.body: Registration is required of men between 18 and 26.

duties.prompt: What is the last day you can send in federal income tax forms?
duties.body: Tax Day — April 15. A responsibility with a deadline.

duties.prompt: What is one promise you make when you become a United States citizen?
answers: give up loyalty to other countries
defend the Constitution and laws of the United States
obey the laws of the United States
serve in the U.S. military (if needed)
serve (do important work for) the nation (if needed)
be loyal to the United States
duties.body: The Oath of Allegiance, in plain words.

duties.prompt: What is one way Americans can participate in their democracy?
answers: give an elected official your opinion on an issue
publicly support or oppose an issue or policy
duties.body: Democracy is a participation sport with many positions.

duties.prompt: What do we show loyalty to when we say the Pledge of Allegiance?
duties.body: The flag, and the republic for which it stands.

reading.title: The Tenth Amendment
reading.body: Powers not delegated to the United States, nor prohibited to the states, are reserved to the states — or to the people. Eleven words that started every states' rights argument since 1791.

reading.title: Federalism
reading.body: One country, two full governments over every citizen: national and state. Each has its own laws, courts, and taxes. The Constitution is the referee.

reading.title: The Supremacy Clause
reading.body: When a valid federal law and a state law collide, federal law wins — Article VI calls the Constitution 'the supreme Law of the Land.'

reading.title: Reserved Powers
reading.body: Schools, police, licenses, marriage, zoning, most criminal law — the everyday machinery of life is run by states because the Constitution never gave it to Washington.

reading.title: Concurrent Powers
reading.body: Some powers are shared: taxing, borrowing, building roads, running courts. Two governments, both with their hands in your wallet, legally.

reading.title: Full Faith and Credit
reading.body: Article IV makes states honor each other's public acts, records, and court judgments — your license and your marriage travel with you across state lines.

reading.title: State Constitutions
reading.body: Every state has its own constitution — most are longer than the federal one, and several are older. States are laboratories with their own rulebooks.

reading.title: McCulloch v. Maryland (1819)
reading.body: Maryland tried to tax the national bank. Chief Justice Marshall said no: implied federal powers are real, and 'the power to tax involves the power to destroy.'
